studies.title: Works Lost, A State Set Right
studies.meaning: The surah opens with two sentences built as mirrors, and the mirroring is exact enough to be the argument. On one side, two acts are named, refusing and turning others away, and the consequence falls not on the people but on their works, which are said to go missing. On the other side, three acts are named, and two consequences follow: wrongs are covered over, and something is put right. The word for what is put right is unusual, glossed by commentators as a person's whole condition, his affairs and his state of mind together.
studies.historicalContext: Medinan, from the years after the emigration when the community in Medina was in open conflict with the city it had left. The surah's opening does not describe that conflict directly; it sets out the terms on which the two sides are being described, which is why it deals with the fate of deeds rather than with events. The commentators report no single occasion for these two ayat.

keyTerms.note: Literally to cause something to be lost, the verb used of a man who loses his camel in open country. Applied to works it pictures effort that goes astray rather than effort that is punished.
To cover a thing so it cannot be seen. It shares a root with the word for concealing the truth, so the same action is named differently depending on who does it and to what.
A word for the whole of a person's situation, his affairs and his mind at once, with no single English equivalent. It occurs twice in the Quran, both times in this surah, a few ayat apart.

studies.lifeInProphetsTime: Losing something in the desert was a specific and familiar disaster. A camel that wandered off at night might be alive somewhere and still be gone for good, since the country was too large to search. Traders lost goods the same way, on a road they could not retrace. The image behind the first sentence is not confiscation but that kind of loss, where the thing still exists and can no longer be reached.
studies.didYouKnow: The Prophet Muhammad (peace be upon him) is named by that name only four times in the whole Quran. Two of those occurrences are in this pair of surahs: here, and again in the closing ayah of the surah that follows. The other two are in earlier Medinan chapters, one about mortality and one about his standing among the prophets.
studies.theologicalSignificance: The passage turns attention away from persons and onto what they produce, which is a distinctive move. Nobody is described as being destroyed in either sentence; deeds are lost in the first and a condition is repaired in the second. That keeps the judgement about outcomes rather than about worth, and it makes the object of hope specific. What is promised is not a feeling but a state that has been set right, which is something a person can be in without knowing it.

crossReferences.why: Shows the same fate for works from the other side: deeds turned into scattered dust.
Carries the other naming of the Prophet, and describes those with him by their marks and conduct.
Repeats the promise about their state a few ayat later, using the same unusual word.

studies.applyIt: Think about one piece of work you put real effort into that came to nothing. A project cancelled, a relationship you tried hard in. Sit with how that felt, exactly, and then read the first sentence of this surah again. The image is precise, and precision about loss is more useful than being told it did not matter.

studies.title: Both Sides Are Following
studies.meaning: The explanation offered for the contrast just drawn uses one verb twice, and that repetition is the whole point. Both groups follow. Neither is described as thinking while the other does not, and no one here is called stupid. The difference is entirely in what walks ahead. The word rendered as falsehood does not primarily mean inaccurate; it means void, what has no substance and cannot bear weight. The closing clause then names the method: these portraits are being set out for people, which makes the two preceding sentences examples rather than verdicts.
studies.historicalContext: Medinan. The surah addresses a community that had recently become a society, with converts, neighbours, allies and opponents living in proximity and sorting themselves out. Descriptions of two paths carried practical weight in that setting, since people were making decisions about where they stood. No specific occasion is reported for this ayah; the commentators read it as the reason attached to the surah's opening pair.

keyTerms.note: To walk behind, originally to go after tracks in the ground. Using it of both groups puts the entire difference in what is out in front, not in the fact or the manner of following.

From a root meaning to come to nothing, to lapse, to be null. It is the empty as opposed to the substantial rather than the inaccurate as opposed to the correct, and it names a thing that will not hold.

A comparison offered so that something can be seen. Attaching the plural to them turns the two descriptions just given into portraits held up for an audience rather than sentences passed on individuals.

studies.lifeInProphetsTime: Tracking was a real skill and a respected one. A man could read from prints in the sand how many animals had passed, how heavily laden, how long ago, and disputes were settled by people who did this professionally. Following tracks meant committing to someone else's route before you could see where it ended. That is the picture underneath the verb, and it makes the choice a practical one rather than an intellectual position.
studies.didYouKnow: The Quran uses the phrase about God setting out likenesses for people as a recurring formula, and it usually appears immediately after a comparison rather than before one. Here it closes a two-line description with no imagery in it at all, which suggests that the plain contrast of two ways of living is itself being offered as the picture.
studies.theologicalSignificance: The passage is unusually generous about human reasoning and unusually severe about its object. Everyone is credited with following something, which grants a kind of seriousness to positions the surah rejects. What is denied is not intelligence but substance, and the vocabulary makes that a claim about reality rather than about people. Where truth is described, it is qualified as coming from their Lord, so the contrast is finally about origin rather than about the quality of anyone's thinking.

crossReferences.why: Draws the same contrast as two trees, one rooted and reaching upward, one uprooted with no stability.
Compares truth and emptiness to water and the froth on it, and says which one remains.
Says these comparisons are set out for people, and that only those with knowledge take hold of them.

studies.applyIt: Name what you are actually walking behind this month. Not your beliefs, your direction: a person whose approval you are chasing, a number, a plan you inherited. Write the honest answer somewhere private. The ayah does not ask you to stop following. It assumes you will not. It asks you to look at what is in front.

studies.title: Until The War Sets Down Its Load
studies.meaning: The ayah describes a sequence for people already in a battle, and most of it is about what happens once the fighting is decided. After the engagement comes a marked turning point, named by a verb meaning that resistance has been broken, and from there the passage is entirely about captives: they are secured, and then two ways out are named, release without payment or release for ransom. A limit is set on the whole thing, phrased as war putting down what it carries. The commentators discuss the scope of the two named options and do not agree.
studies.historicalContext: Medinan, from the years of open war between Medina and the city the emigrants had left. Fighting had not been permitted to the community through the Meccan period, and permission came only after the emigration, when the conflict was already under way. The classical sources report no single occasion for this ayah; they read it as addressing a situation the community was in, and they connect its second half to the disposal of captives after the early engagements.

keyTerms.note: From a root for thickness and weight; the verb describes pressing an opponent until he can no longer hold. It marks a point inside the sequence, after which the ayah speaks only of captives.
The binding itself rather than the act of binding. The word occurs once in the Quran, and its close cognate is the ordinary term for a covenant, so the same root ties both prisoners and promises.
What a beast or a person carries, and by extension an army's arms and gear. War is pictured as something that has been carrying a weight and eventually sets it down.

studies.lifeInProphetsTime: Arabian warfare had its own economy of captives, and ransom was the ordinary channel. A family raised the sum, agents carried it between camps, and the price varied with a man's standing. Reports about the aftermath of the first major battle describe captives held in Medinan households and fed from the same food, with some of them ransoming themselves by teaching children in the town to write. Release without payment was also recorded, and it cost the captor something real.
studies.didYouKnow: This surah carries two names in the classical sources. It is usually called by the name of the Prophet Muhammad (peace be upon him), which appears in its second ayah, and it is also known by a name drawn from the subject of this passage. Very few surahs are commonly known by two names in the tradition, and this is one of them.
studies.theologicalSignificance: The passage refuses one reading of victory before anyone can reach it. God could have dealt with the opposing side directly, it says, and did not; what is happening instead is a testing of people by means of each other. That places both sides inside the same examination and denies either of them the claim that an outcome settles who was favoured. The final clause turns to those killed and promises only that their work will not be lost, which is a narrow and exact reassurance.

crossReferences.why: Addresses captives directly, including what may be found in their hearts and what could be given back.
Places the captive alongside the poor and the orphan among those the righteous are described as feeding.
Sets the boundary the tradition reads alongside this passage: fight those who fight you, without aggression.

studies.applyIt: Notice the next time you win a small argument outright. The moment the other person stops defending is the moment this passage is interested in, and the choice it describes there is between letting go for nothing and asking for something. You will not need a ruling to know which you did. Try the first one, once, this week.

studies.title: Firm Feet On Loose Ground
studies.meaning: The promise in the first two ayat belongs to those killed in God's way in the ayah before: guidance after death, a settled condition, and a garden they will recognise as if they had lived there. Then the address turns to the living with a conditional that reverses the usual direction. God, who needs nothing, describes help given to Him, and the return promised is not victory but firm feet. Steadiness is the thing asked for and the thing given.
studies.historicalContext: Medinan, from the period after the emigration when the community had left Mecca under pressure and was facing organised hostility from it. The surah is named for the Prophet Muhammad (peace be upon him) and several commentators associate it broadly with the years around the first pitched battles, though no specific occasion is reported for these ayat. Its audience is a small community with no experience of war and no reserves.

keyTerms.note: The ordinary word for coming to someone's aid in a fight. Applying it to God is a deliberate shock, since the one aided is the one who needs nothing, and the commentators read it as aiding His cause.
The image is a foot that does not slide on loose ground. Ancient battle turned on whether a line held its footing, so the phrase promises the condition for winning rather than the win.
A word for the condition a person is in and the thoughts that occupy them. Setting it right covers both the outward situation and the inner unrest, which the translation has to choose between.
A verb of acquainting. Classical readers take it either as God describing the garden until it is familiar, or as each person being led to a place already known, like a man walking home.

studies.lifeInProphetsTime: Battle in that world was fought on foot in a shallow line, and the ground mattered. Sand gave way, gravel rolled, and a slope decided who tired first. Commanders chose their footing before they chose their moment, and a line that broke did so by stepping backwards one man at a time. Fighters who had never trained together, which is what the Medina community was, felt that first in their legs.
studies.didYouKnow: The conditional in the seventh ayah repeats the same verb on both sides, so the support offered and the support returned are named with one word. The Quran uses that mirrored shape sparingly. A parallel line in surah 22 makes the same promise as a description rather than a bargain.
studies.theologicalSignificance: God is described as receiving help, which the Quran elsewhere makes impossible, so the phrase has to be read as help to what He has commanded rather than to Him. The commentators say so plainly. What the passage establishes is a shape for divine aid: it is conditional, it is proportionate to effort already spent, and what it delivers is capacity rather than outcome. The one who is helped still has to stand.

crossReferences.why: States the second half of the same promise without a condition: God will support those who support Him.
Runs the conditional in the other direction, making every human aid depend on His support rather than the reverse.
Pairs standing firm with abundant remembrance, naming the practice that the promise of steady feet answers.

studies.applyIt: Take one commitment you made for God's sake that has gone quiet, a fast you kept, a person you were helping, a habit of reading. Do the smallest version of it today, once. This passage does not promise the outcome will change. It promises footing, which is what you notice only when you are still standing at the end of a hard week.

studies.title: One Side Has No Patron
studies.meaning: Three short ayat, each explaining the one before it. First a cause is given, and it is an emotional one rather than an intellectual one: they found what was sent down distasteful. Then an instruction to travel and look at what became of earlier peoples, which asks for evidence that can be walked to. The third supplies the underlying asymmetry, and it does so by using a single word twice, once with something behind it and once with nothing. God is the patron of those who believe; the other side has no patron at all.
studies.historicalContext: Medinan, in a period when the community was surrounded by parties whose loyalties were mixed and shifting. Alliance was the organising fact of Arabian politics, and the surah is describing two positions in terms an audience of that time understood as political as much as religious. The commentators report no specific occasion for these ayat, and read them as the explanation attached to the surah's opening contrast.

keyTerms.note: A verb of aversion rather than of judgement. It names a reaction of the appetite, which locates the refusal described here below the level of argument, in what a person cannot stand.

A word covering the whole relationship of protection between a strong party and one under his care, in both directions. The ayah uses it twice, once with a party behind it and once with an empty space.
From a root for what follows behind, as a heel follows a step. It names not the final judgement but the visible end of a course of action, which is why the ayah says go and look.

studies.lifeInProphetsTime: Patronage was the load-bearing structure of that society. A freed slave kept a formal tie to the family that freed him; a weaker clan bound itself to a stronger one; a stranger in a town needed someone to answer for him. The word used here covers all of those relationships. To say a group has no patron was not a religious insult but a description of complete exposure, and everyone hearing it knew what it looked like.
studies.didYouKnow: The instruction to travel through the land and look at the outcome of earlier peoples is a fixed formula in the Quran. This exact wording appears four times, always as a question rather than a command, and always aimed at people who had the ruins within reach. It treats archaeology, in effect, as an argument available to anyone willing to make the journey.
studies.theologicalSignificance: The middle ayah makes a claim about how evidence works that is easy to miss. What is offered is not a miracle but a pattern, visible in the ordinary record of collapsed civilisations, and the reader is asked to go and see it for himself. The outer two ayat then place that pattern inside a relationship. What decides an outcome, in this account, is not strength or numbers but whether anything stands behind you, and only one of the two sides is said to have that.

crossReferences.why: Gives the same instruction to travel and look, and locates the failure in hearts rather than eyes.
States the positive half directly: God is your patron, and the best of helpers.
Describes earlier peoples who were stronger and worked the land more thoroughly, and what followed.

studies.applyIt: Notice the difference between disagreeing with something and not being able to stand it. The first ayah here names the second. If there is a teaching or a person you avoid with a feeling in your stomach rather than an argument in your head, sit with the feeling for a minute today without settling it. Recognising an aversion is not the same as obeying it.

studies.title: As The Cattle Eat
studies.meaning: The comparison in the middle of the first ayah is doing all the work. One group is described by where it is going; the other is described by what it does with its days, and the description is deliberately unelevated. They take their pleasure and they eat the way grazing animals eat. Nothing there is called wicked. What is denied is any horizon beyond the next mouthful. The second ayah then turns to address the listener directly, in the second person, about the town that drove him out and about towns stronger than it that are gone.
studies.historicalContext: Medinan. The classical sources connect the second of these ayat to the emigration, and several report it as revealed in connection with the departure from Mecca, though they differ over the exact circumstance. The address is unusually personal for this surah: it names the listener's own town and the fact of his expulsion from it, then places that town on a list of settlements that had more power and are no longer there.

keyTerms.note: A form implying the taking of a portion for a limited term. The root gives the word for provisions carried on a journey, so pleasure is described as something drawn down rather than possessed.
The word for camels, cattle, sheep and goats together. The Quran usually speaks of them as a favour and a provision, which makes their appearance here as a comparison unusually pointed.
From a root for staying put, used of the place a traveller settles at the end of a stage. Set against the previous clause about eating, it supplies the destination the description had left out.

studies.lifeInProphetsTime: Every household in that world lived close to its animals. People knew exactly what a herd's day looked like: the animals ate what was in front of them, moved when the grazing thinned, and showed no sign of a plan. Livestock was also wealth, so the comparison is not contempt for the animals themselves. It is an observation about a way of spending a day that everyone present had watched from a few paces away, every morning.
studies.didYouKnow: The word used here for a lodging place is an ordinary travellers' term for where you put up at the end of a stage. The Quran attaches it to the Fire in several places, but it also uses it in the story of Joseph, where a household in Egypt is told to make his lodging generous, and again a few ayat further on in this same surah for simply where people dwell.
studies.theologicalSignificance: The passage measures a life by its horizon rather than by its morals, which is an uncommon test. What separates the two groups in the first ayah is not that one behaves badly, since no misdeed is named, but that one of them has a description that runs past this afternoon. The second ayah adds the same point at the scale of cities. Power is real and produces nothing durable, and the listener is asked to hold that thought about the place that expelled him.

crossReferences.why: Uses the same comparison and pushes it further, saying they are more astray than grazing animals.
Repeats the image for those with hearts, eyes and ears that they do not use for understanding.
Asks the same question about earlier peoples who were stronger and left more traces behind them.

studies.applyIt: Write down what you did yesterday, hour by hour, without editing. Then look at whether any of it points past next week. This is not an accusation; most days are maintenance, and maintenance is necessary. The ayah is only asking whether a description of your day would need a horizon in it at all, and yesterday is the honest sample.

studies.title: When Your Own Deed Looks Good
studies.meaning: The question compares two positions, and the grammar of the second one is where the difficulty lies. The first man stands on something that came from outside him, a clear proof from his Lord. The second is described in the passive: his bad deed was made to look attractive to him. No agent is named, which the commentators discuss without settling, and the effect of leaving it unnamed is that the man cannot locate the source of his own approval. The sentence then widens from a single figure to a plural, and ends on desires being followed.
studies.historicalContext: Medinan. The surah is describing a society in which people held positions of very different kinds, some settled, some shifting, some concealed. That setting explains why the ayah is framed as a comparison rather than a verdict: it is offering a way of telling two conditions apart from the inside. The commentators report no particular occasion, and read it as introducing the contrast the following ayah develops at length.

keyTerms.note: Something that makes itself evident and clarifies what is near it. Standing upon it is a posture of resting weight on a surface, so the metaphor is of a footing rather than of a belief held in the head.

A passive form with no agent named. The verb is used of decorating something so it attracts, and the passive leaves the person unable to say who did the decorating, which is the state being described.
A plural from a root meaning to fall or to descend. What it names is not desire in general but the pull of a particular leaning, and the plural suggests several of them at once.

studies.lifeInProphetsTime: A trader's whole livelihood rested on being able to tell a dressed-up thing from a sound one. Animals were fattened and oiled before market, dates packed with the best fruit on top, cloth folded to hide a flaw. Buyers developed habits of checking, and a man who could not was pitied. The image behind this ayah comes from that world: something has been made attractive, and the question is whether the person looking can tell.
studies.didYouKnow: The Quran uses this verb for making something look attractive in two constructions. Ten times it appears in the agentless passive form used here, where nothing is said about who did it. More often it appears in an active form with an agent named, and the agent named is not always the same one. Both constructions run through the Book side by side.
studies.theologicalSignificance: The passage locates the danger inside approval rather than inside temptation. Someone who knows he is doing wrong is not described here at all; the figure in question finds his own act genuinely appealing, which removes the friction that would ordinarily warn him. What is offered against that is not stronger willpower but an external footing, something from his Lord that he did not generate. The contrast is therefore between two sources of assessment, not between two levels of effort.

crossReferences.why: Asks about the same figure directly: is one whose evil deed is made attractive so that he sees it as good.
Describes those whose effort went astray while they thought they were doing excellent work.
Shows the same process arriving after hardship, when what they were doing was made appealing to them.

studies.applyIt: Take one habit you have already justified to yourself, fluently, more than once. The fluency is the thing to notice, not the habit. Explanations that arrive quickly and completely are usually older than the situation they explain. You do not have to change it today. Just observe how ready the defence was, and where you learned it.

studies.title: Four Rivers, Four Corrections
studies.meaning: Four rivers are named and each carries a qualifying phrase, and the qualifications are what the passage is actually about. Water that does not go stale, milk whose taste does not turn, wine that is a pleasure to those who drink it, honey that has been strained clear. Each clause names the exact way the earthly version fails. Then forgiveness is listed alongside the fruit, as one item among the provisions rather than as a separate category. The comparison at the end is left grammatically unfinished, which the commentators note.
studies.historicalContext: Medinan. The surah has just asked whether two people can be alike, and this ayah answers by describing the two conditions rather than by arguing. Descriptions of paradise in the Medinan surahs tend to arrive inside comparisons of this kind. The classical commentators report no specific occasion, and they read the passage as the extended half of the question raised immediately before it.

keyTerms.note: Used of standing water that has turned and smells. The word occurs once in the Quran, and it names the specific fear of anyone drawing from a cistern at the end of a dry season.
Filtered so that nothing solid remains. Honey taken from a wild comb carries wax, bark and dead bees, and the word answers that directly. It occurs once in the Quran.
The word opening the ayah signals that what follows is a comparison offered to convey something, not a survey. Commentators have leaned on it heavily when discussing how the details are to be taken.

studies.lifeInProphetsTime: Every item on this list was a real anxiety. Cisterns and skins went bad, and water carried on a journey was drunk warm and tasting of the hide. Milk soured within hours in that heat. Wild honey was cut from rock crevices and came out full of comb and grit. Fruit arrived in a season and was gone. The description is not exotic luxury; it is the ordinary provision of that world with each of its known failures removed.
studies.didYouKnow: Three of the words in this ayah occur nowhere else in the Quran: the term for water gone stale, the word for honey strained clear, and the word for what the boiling drink does to the bowels at the end. A single ayah carrying three words unique to it is unusual, and all three of them are doing precisely the same job, naming a specific physical detail.
studies.theologicalSignificance: Placing forgiveness in the middle of a list of provisions is the passage's most deliberate move. It is not offered as the condition for the rest or as a spiritual counterweight to the physical items; it is another thing they are given. That treats pardon as a kind of sustenance, something a person continues to receive rather than a transaction completed at the gate. The unfinished comparison at the end leaves the other half of the sentence for the reader to supply.

crossReferences.why: Opens with the identical formula about the garden promised to the righteous, then describes food and shade without end.
Describes a drink in the garden from a named spring, alongside the drinking vessels and the setting.
Lists what is carried round to them, including a drink that causes neither headache nor intoxication.

studies.applyIt: Notice how much of your day is spent managing spoilage. Food that will turn, a battery draining, a relationship that needs maintaining or it drifts. The ayah's four clauses are all about that one problem. Pick one thing today you keep having to top up, and let the effort of it register instead of irritating you.

studies.title: What Did He Say Just Now
studies.meaning: The scene is small and exact. Some of them sit and listen, and then on the way out ask the people with knowledge what was just said. The question is not hostile. It is worse than hostile, because nothing at all was retained from a session they had physically attended. The verdict names a sealing of hearts, and the same clause about following one's inclinations that closed the previous comparison. Then the other half arrives, and it is not symmetrical: those already guided are increased in guidance, and given the very awareness that keeps them.
studies.historicalContext: Medinan. Gatherings for recitation and teaching were open in Medina, and people attended for a range of reasons, some of them social or political rather than religious. The commentators read this ayah as describing that mixture rather than a single incident, and they identify the people with knowledge as those in the same gathering who had actually held on to what was said. No specific occasion is reliably reported.

keyTerms.note: From the word for the nose, the foremost part, so it means the nearest past. It occurs once in the Quran, and its precision is the point: they are asking about something that ended seconds earlier.
The verb for pressing a seal into clay or wax to close a document. What it describes is not damage but closure, a container that has been shut and marked so that nothing more goes in.
A state of careful protectiveness, from a root for shielding oneself. The possessive is striking: it is theirs, and the ayah says it was given to them, both at once.

studies.lifeInProphetsTime: That was an oral culture with formidable standards of retention. Men held long odes in memory after a single hearing, genealogies were carried for generations, and legal arrangements were witnessed rather than written. Failing to retain what had just been recited in a gathering was not an ordinary lapse in that setting. It would have been noticed by everyone present, which is why the question is described as being asked outside, on the way out.
studies.didYouKnow: The word for just now in this ayah is the only occurrence of that form in the Quran. So is the phrase in the following ayah about being increased in guidance. Two consecutive ayat each carrying a form that appears nowhere else is rare, and the two halves of the contrast are marked by it, one for what was lost and one for what was added.
studies.theologicalSignificance: The two ayat together describe momentum rather than status. On one side a seal, which stops further entry; on the other an increase, which implies a starting point already reached. Neither is presented as an arbitrary allocation, since each follows from what the person was already doing with what they had. The last clause complicates any simple account of effort: their guardedness is called theirs and is also said to be given, and the passage does not resolve the tension.

crossReferences.why: Uses the same verb for a sealing of hearts and hearing, with a covering placed over the sight.
Shows the same increase, describing young men who believed and were given more guidance.
Describes a chapter arriving and increasing belief in some while adding defilement to others.

studies.applyIt: After the next thing you listen to properly, a talk, a recitation, a friend telling you something difficult, wait five minutes and then say one sentence of it back to yourself. If nothing comes, that is information, not failure. The ayah is describing an ordinary human experience precisely, and noticing it is the first thing that changes it.

studies.title: Its Tokens Have Already Come
studies.meaning: A question is asked that is not really a question: are they waiting for the Hour to arrive on them without warning. Then a statement that cuts against the waiting, since its signs have already come. The word used for those signs means conditions or markers, the small indications that something is under way, and it occurs only here. The last clause is a piece of grammar rather than a threat. When the thing arrives, what use would remembering be to them, since the point of a reminder is that there is still time.
studies.historicalContext: Medinan. The surah has just contrasted people who retained nothing from a gathering with people whose guidance increased, and this ayah follows immediately. The commentators generally read the markers as including the arrival of the message itself and the splitting of the community's responses to it, though they record more than one view. No particular occasion is reported for the ayah.

keyTerms.note: A plural for signs that something is under way, related to the word for a stipulated condition in an agreement. It occurs once in the Quran, and it names indications rather than proofs.
An adverb for something arriving with no approach, the way a creditor appears at a door. It is used repeatedly in the Quran of the Hour, and always from the perspective of the unprepared.
A noun for the act of recollecting rather than for the thing recalled. Attaching it to them makes it their own remembering, which is what the closing clause says will no longer be of use.

studies.lifeInProphetsTime: People in that world read approaching events from small indications constantly. A change in the wind, dust on a horizon, the behaviour of camels before a storm, the first traders back from a season with news. Nobody waited for an event to arrive before preparing for it, because in a place with no shelter, arrival was already too late. The ayah uses that habit of reading indications and asks why it has been suspended here.
studies.didYouKnow: The word for the markers of the Hour occurs exactly once in the Quran, in this ayah, and the Quran never lists what they are. The extensive later literature on the signs of the Hour is built almost entirely from reports outside the Book. What the Quran itself says here is only that some of them have already arrived.
studies.theologicalSignificance: The ayah's real subject is the structure of a warning. A reminder is defined by the interval it opens, so the same words that were useful yesterday become empty at the moment they are confirmed. That places the whole value of a warning in the period before anything is settled, which is exactly the period the reader occupies. It also says something modest about signs: they are markers rather than proofs, enough to prompt attention and not enough to compel it.

crossReferences.why: Says the Hour will come upon them suddenly, and that its knowledge rests with God alone.
Describes the same arrival without warning, and the regret expressed at that moment for what was neglected.
Urges following the best of what was sent down before the punishment comes suddenly and unperceived.

studies.applyIt: Think of something you already know is coming and have made no arrangement for. A conversation, a bill, a health thing you have noticed. The ayah is not asking you to feel afraid. It is pointing at the gap between having the information and acting on it, and that gap closes with one small task today.

studies.title: Know First, Then Ask Pardon
studies.meaning: The command is to know, not to say, and what follows knowledge is asking forgiveness. The order is deliberate: the deeper the recognition of God, the more visible one's own shortfall. The Prophet Muhammad (peace be upon him) is addressed first and then told to seek forgiveness for the whole community, men and women named separately. The closing clause covers a whole life in two words, where you move by day and where you settle at night.
studies.historicalContext: Medinan, in a surah addressed to a community under military pressure and containing several portraits of people whose commitment was thin. The ayah lands right after a description of listeners who left the Prophet's presence and asked each other what he had just said. No specific occasion is reported. The instruction to seek forgiveness for the believers puts the leader's own prayer at the community's service.

keyTerms.note: An imperative of knowledge rather than of speech. The classical readers stress that what is asked is a settled recognition, the kind you act from, not a formula recited, and the rest of the ayah follows from it.
Built from a root meaning to turn something over. It covers travelling, trading, restlessness in bed, and the turns a life takes, so the word for daily activity is also the word for upheaval.
The place a traveller stops and stays. Paired with the word for movement, it splits existence in two, and the pairing is used elsewhere of both the grave and the final abode.

studies.lifeInProphetsTime: A merchant's year had exactly these two halves. He was on the road with the caravan, turning goods over in markets from Yemen to Syria, or he was at home in the settlement waiting out the season. Arabic had a natural pair of words for it, and everyone listening knew which half of the year they were in. The ayah takes that pair and says both halves are watched.
studies.didYouKnow: An early hadith collection heads its chapter on knowledge with the opening words of this ayah, using them to argue that knowing comes before speaking and acting. The chapter title is one of the shortest arguments in that literature: the imperative in the ayah is to know, and every instruction in the sentence comes after it.
studies.theologicalSignificance: Two things sit oddly together here and the tradition holds them together. The one addressed is the recipient of revelation, and he is still told to seek forgiveness, which the commentators explain as a difference of degree rather than of kind: the nearer the servant, the finer the shortfall he can see. The ayah also makes intercession ordinary. Asking pardon for other people is presented as part of a believing life, not a special office.

crossReferences.why: Places the same forgiveness for the Prophet inside the announcement of a victory, in the surah that follows this one.
Ends the mission with the same instruction, praise and seeking pardon, at the moment of complete success.
Shows believers asking pardon for others by name, continuing the practice this ayah assigns to the community's leader.

studies.applyIt: Before you sleep, ask forgiveness once for someone else by name, and do not tell them. Choose a person you are slightly annoyed with rather than one you love, because the ayah pairs the request with a community that was not uniformly loyal. Notice what asking on their behalf does to how you plan to speak to them tomorrow.

studies.title: Until The Claim Becomes Fact
studies.meaning: The testing is stated as certain, and its purpose is given in a form that has troubled readers: until We know. The commentators are united that God's knowledge is not increased, and read the phrase as knowledge becoming actual in the world, the difference between what a person is and what a person has done. The last clause widens it further. Not only conduct is tested but what is reported of you, the account your life gives.
studies.historicalContext: Medinan, at the close of a surah that has spent its last section on people inside the community whose loyalty was uncertain. The ayah immediately before says they will be known by the way they talk. No specific occasion is reported. In the years after the emigration, the community was mixed by circumstance rather than conviction, and pressure was the only thing that separated its parts.

keyTerms.note: The verb is used of trying metal and of wearing something out with use. Two emphatic particles are attached, one before and one after, so the sentence admits no possibility that testing might be skipped.

An active participle from a root meaning exertion to the limit of capacity. It covers effort of every kind against difficulty, and the passage pairs it immediately with endurance rather than with success.
The word for tidings and for what is said about someone in their absence. Testing your news means testing the record, so the object examined is not only the act but the story it leaves.

studies.lifeInProphetsTime: Reputation in Arabia travelled faster than any person could. A man's news reached the next oasis with the first rider, and it was all a stranger had to judge him by. Tribes kept the record in poetry: who held a line, who ran, who paid a debt. To have your news tested was to have the thing you could not control examined, since you did not compose it and could not correct it.
studies.didYouKnow: The phrase until We know appears in several places in the Quran, usually after a description of hardship, and it drew a standing note from the classical grammarians. They read the verb as knowledge coming into view rather than knowledge acquired. The comparison usually offered is a teacher who already knows the answer and sets the paper anyway.
studies.theologicalSignificance: The ayah makes trial structural rather than incidental. It is not a response to wrongdoing and not a sign of disfavour; it is the method by which a claim becomes a fact. Two qualities are named as what the testing looks for, effort and endurance, and neither is an outcome. That leaves the believer's part defined by what can be attempted rather than by what can be achieved, which is the only part anyone actually holds.

crossReferences.why: Opens another surah with the same premise, that a profession of faith is never left unexamined.
Names the specific forms the testing takes and attaches the promise of good news to endurance.
Uses the same two words, strivers and the steadfast, in the same construction, and attaches them to entering the garden.

studies.applyIt: Think about the last time something went wrong at work or at home, and ask yourself only one question: what did the first hour of it look like from outside. Not whether you were right. What someone watching would have written down. This ayah says the record is part of the test, and the record is made in the first hour.
